analysis.one_liner: Bans drug middlemen from pocketing spreads and clawbacks, and forces disclosure of their fees and rebates.
analysis.headline: Introduced February 2025 with 15 senators from both parties behind it, the bill has sat in the Senate Commerce Committee ever since without a markup or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it illegal for pharmacy benefit managers — the middlemen who run drug benefits for insurers and employers — to charge a health plan more for a drug than they pay the pharmacy and keep the difference. It also bans arbitrary clawbacks of pharmacy reimbursements, requires annual public reporting of PBMs' fees, spreads, and rebate deals to federal regulators, protects whistleblowers who report abuses, and lets the Federal Trade Commission fine violators up to $1 million per violation, with each day counted separately.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who fill prescriptions, since hidden markups and opaque rebate deals are a documented driver of what they pay at the counter; independent and community pharmacies, which lose money when PBMs claw back reimbursements or underpay them; employers, unions, and insurers that buy drug benefits and would finally see what the middleman charges and keeps; and taxpayers, because Medicare and Medicaid pay PBMs through the same opaque system. Employees at PBMs, pharmacies, and drug companies also gain legal protection for reporting abuses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, independent pharmacies, and health plans

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits 'spread pricing': a PBM can no longer charge a health plan more for a drug's cost or dispensing fee than it reimburses the pharmacy while keeping the difference — unless it passes 100% of every price concession back to the plan and fully discloses its fees and markups.

Bars PBMs from arbitrarily, unfairly, or deceptively reducing or clawing back reimbursement payments to pharmacies, and from raising pharmacy fees to offset federal reimbursement changes — a practice that has pushed independent pharmacies toward closure.

Requires every PBM to report annually to the FTC and Health and Human Services: the spread between what plans pay and pharmacies receive, fees charged to pharmacies, clawbacks, the reason any drug was moved to a tier with higher patient costs, and whether PBMs pay their own pharmacies better than outside ones.

Orders a GAO study of how much of each rebate actually reaches patients versus payors versus the PBM, for each of the 10 largest PBMs, plus prior-authorization delays and whether formularies favor high-rebate drugs over cheaper alternatives.

Protects whistleblowers: no PBM, pharmacy, insurer, or drugmaker may fire, demote, or retaliate against employees who report violations, and workers can sue for reinstatement, double back pay, and damages — rights that cannot be waived by forced arbitration.

Gives the FTC enforcement power over PBMs (including nonprofits and insurance businesses it normally cannot touch), civil penalties up to $1 million per violation with each day a separate violation, and lets state attorneys general sue in federal court on behalf of residents.
Explicitly preserves stronger state PBM laws rather than overriding them.

analysis.who_pays: The large pharmacy benefit managers — the three biggest (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, and Optum Rx) control most of the market — would lose revenue from spreads and clawbacks, face new annual reporting and compliance costs, and risk FTC fines of up to $1 million per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately. Insurers and employers could see some compliance costs passed through to them.

drawbacks.text: The spread-pricing ban has a large exception: a PBM may keep charging plans more than it pays pharmacies if it passes along 100% of price concessions and discloses everything. In practice, the ban depends on the disclosure being complete and accurate, which turns the core prohibition into a compliance test rather than a flat ban.

PBMs get an affirmative defense: conduct that looks like a violation is allowed if the company proves it was nonpretextual and reasonably necessary to comply with law, protect patient safety, or protect patient access — broad categories that could swallow much of the ban in litigation.

The bill does not cap drug prices or patient copays directly; relief for consumers is indirect and depends on FTC enforcement, annual reports, and market response. The $1 million-per-violation penalty cap is a modest sum for companies that process billions of prescriptions a year.
Annual disclosure and reporting requirements create compliance costs for PBMs and pharmacies alike, some portion of which could be passed through to health plans and premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The pharmacy protections, whistleblower rights, and disclosure requirements are real and enforceable, and the bill strengthens rather than overrides state law. But its direct effect on what patients pay is uncertain: the central ban is softened by a full-disclosure exception and a broad affirmative defense, and there are no direct price or copay caps. An honest supporter would say this is a transparency-and-enforcement bill whose savings for consumers depend heavily on the FTC actually using its new powers.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in February 2025 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Grassley introduced the bill on February 11, 2025, joined by 11 original cosponsors including Senator Maria Cantwell and senators from both parties.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
The action history shows no markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor action since the February 2025 referral, while the Congress remains in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large pharmacy benefit managers: with no committee or floor action, the spread pricing, clawbacks, and opaque rebate deals the bill targets continue unchanged, while patients and pharmacies get no new protections yet.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship splits 9 Republicans and 6 Democrats, including Iowa's two senators; there has been no vote to show how the full chambers would line up.

industries.note: The bill attacks the core of PBM revenue: spread pricing (charging plans more than pharmacies are paid and keeping the difference), clawbacks of pharmacy reimbursements, and hidden fees and rebates. It forces annual disclosure to the FTC and HHS and adds fines up to $1 million per violation. The three largest PBMs process most U.S. prescriptions, so the stakes are concentrated in very few companies.

Pharmacies would be protected from arbitrary clawbacks and fee increases, and PBMs would have to report whether they pay their own affiliated pharmacies better than outside ones. Independent pharmacies, which have closed in large numbers citing PBM underpayment, would get the most direct relief.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: Plans would receive full disclosure of what the PBM charges, marks up, and receives from drugmakers, and PBMs must pass 100% of price concessions back to them. That strengthens their negotiating hand but also makes them responsible for scrutinizing the disclosures.

The bill requires disclosure of the total rebates and fees PBMs receive for each drug and a GAO study of how rebates flow, ending some of the secrecy manufacturers and PBMs both rely on. Beyond transparency, their rebate deals are not restricted.

analysis.trajectory: The Congress is still in session. With no committee action since February 2025, a standalone Senate floor vote looks unlikely; PBM bills more often move when attached to a larger package that must pass. The 15-senator bipartisan base keeps it a plausible candidate for a Commerce Committee markup or as an amendment to health or spending legislation, but momentum has stalled for now.
